title: Nominative and accusative: subject and object

objectives.can: Tell a nominative from an accusative and say which is subject and which is object.
Recognise ten of the commonest nouns of the Latin Bible.

explanation.summary: A Latin noun changes its ending to show its job in the clause. The nominative is the case of the subject, and of the noun that completes the verb *sum*. The accusative is the case of the direct object. This lesson teaches how to tell them apart.

sections.heading: Case, number and gender
body: A Latin noun has three properties. Its gender (masculine, feminine or neuter) belongs to the word and does not change: *terra* is feminine and *filius* masculine. Its number (singular or plural) says how many. Its case says what the noun is doing in the clause. Number and case are shown together by the ending.

Latin has six cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative and vocative. This lesson takes the first of the cases that every sentence needs, the nominative, and the accusative. Lessons L1.1.2 and L1.1.3 take the rest.

sections.heading: The nominative: subject and predicate noun
body: The subject of a verb stands in the nominative: in *vidit Deus lucem*, God saw the light, *Deus* is nominative. The nominative is also the case of a noun that completes the verb *sum* ('to be'), because *sum* does not act on anything: it only says that two things are the same. In *Ego sum pastor bonus*, 'I am the good shepherd', *ego* and *pastor* are both nominative, and *pastor* is called the predicate nominative.
A name or a title standing on its own is often nominative as well. The notice on the cross in John 19:19 is written *Jesus Nazarenus, Rex Judæorum*, and *Rex* is nominative.

sections.heading: The accusative: object
body: The direct object of a verb, the thing acted upon, stands in the accusative: in the same clause *lucem* is accusative, 'the light'. The accusative is also the case that many prepositions take, for example *ad* ('to'), *per* ('through') and *super* ('over', 'upon'): *ad Patrem*, *per ipsum*, *super crucem*.

The accusative singular of most nouns ends in -m: -am, -um, -em. The plural ends in -s: -as, -os, -es. The table lists the commonest nominative and accusative endings; the declensions are taught in full in L1.2.1 to L1.2.3.

sections.heading: When the endings agree
body: A neuter noun has the same form in the nominative and the accusative, in both numbers: *verbum* is 'the word' as subject and 'the word' as object, and the plural *verba* serves for both. Only the sentence shows which. In the plural of the third declension the nominative and accusative also coincide in the ending -es.

The texts in this library are analysed automatically, and the analyser often leaves a form undecided between cases (a word like *Verbum* may be listed as nominative, vocative or accusative). The exercises below use only words with a single certain reading, which is why neuter nouns seldom come up. When you read a real verse, use the verb: a noun that does the action is the nominative, and a noun that receives it is the accusative.
In John 1:1, *Verbum erat apud Deum* ('the Word was with God'), *Verbum* is the subject of *erat*, so it is nominative; *Deum* after the preposition *apud* is accusative.

sections.heading: Ten nouns to learn
body: The vocabulary of this lesson is ten of the commonest nouns of the Latin Bible. Learn each with its gender, because adjectives and pronouns will agree with it. *Deus* is masculine, *dominus* masculine, *homo* masculine (it means any human being), *terra* feminine, *filius* masculine, *rex* masculine, *populus* masculine, *verbum* neuter, *manus* feminine, and *dies* masculine or feminine in the singular.

misunderstandings: The noun after *sum* is not an object. *Ego sum pastor* has no accusative: *pastor* is nominative, in the same case as *ego*.
Position does not make a subject. The noun that comes first, or right after the verb, is not for that reason the subject or the object. Check the ending.
The ending -m is not a plural. It usually marks an accusative singular. The plural accusative ends in -s (-as, -os, -es).
A noun without a separate word for 'the' can still be definite. Latin has no article; the English edition shows how the translator took it.

deeper.heading: Why neuters share a form
body: In the inherited ancestor of Latin the neuter nominative and accusative were already identical, and the neuter plural in -a was originally a collective form. That is why the pattern holds in every declension. The older grammars simply state it as a rule: a neuter nominative is always the same as its accusative.

quoted.english: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *pastor* is nominative in both sentences. In *Ego sum pastor bonus* it completes *sum*, so it is a predicate nominative, in the same case as *ego*. In *Bonus pastor animam suam dat* it is the subject of *dat*, and *animam*, with its accusative -am, is the object: 'the good shepherd gives his life'.

examples.analysis: *divisitque* is "and he divided", with *-que* for "and". Its object is *aquas*, accusative plural: the ending -as is the plural counterpart of -am. The subject *Deus* stands in the nominative, and *fecit Deus firmamentum* at the start of the verse has the same pattern: verb, subject, object.
